CREATORS.summary: Ads were still made almost entirely by independent full-service agencies paid out of a 15% media commission. Two things changed inside the era. First, the legal scaffolding that enforced the commission came down: on 1 February 1956 a federal consent decree ended the trade associations' collective 'recognition' machinery, under which publisher groups and the AAAA jointly policed which agencies could receive commission and forbade rebating it to clients. The rate survived anyway, because individual media stayed free to grant or withhold it, and commission remained the dominant compensation mode for decades (71% of large national advertisers still used it in 1982). Second, the work itself changed. Agencies lost the job of producing network programmes to the networks, and gained the job of making 60-second and then 30-second films. The creative revolution - Doyle Dane Bernbach's Volkswagen work from 1959, then Papert Koenig Lois, Wells Rich Greene and Ogilvy - made the copywriter/art-director team, not the account man, the agency's product, and it made small creative shops competitive with giants for the first time. Structurally the era invented the holding company: Interpublic was incorporated in January 1961 so Marion Harper could own competing agencies through separate subsidiaries. By the early 1970s clients were pressing agencies to unbundle, and 'a la carte' creative shops and media-buying services appeared - the first crack in the bundled full-service model that era 4 and era 6 finish breaking.

BUYERS.summary: Four pools of money bought advertising in this era, and they behaved differently. National brand advertisers - packaged goods (Procter & Gamble above all), cars, tobacco, drugs, food - were the marginal new buyer class in the sense that they stopped buying programmes and started buying audiences: a brand manager with a media budget could now assemble reach out of dozens of 30-second units across many shows instead of owning one show. Local retailers bought newspapers first, radio second and television third; their money grew faster than national money after 1970. Classified was bought by individuals and small businesses at a per-line rate with no agency involved - the era's only self-serve, intent-matched, priced-per-unit advertising, and the direct ancestor of paid search. Direct response was bought by mail-order firms and by brands running keyed coupons; it ran through direct mail, which was the single largest national medium in 1975. The striking fact is how little the mix moved: the four pools held 43/36/7/14 percent of US spend in 1950 and 40/38/8/15 percent in 1975. Television's rise from 3% to 19% of all spend was a reallocation inside national brand money - away from radio, magazines and national newspaper space - not a change in what kinds of money existed. Regulation moved one large buyer category out of broadcasting: from 2 January 1971 cigarette makers, who had been paying broadcasters roughly $225 million a year, could no longer buy television or radio at all.

SELLERS.summary: The era's decisive ownership change is that the networks took the inventory back. Before 1950 an advertiser and its agency owned the programme and bought the time around it; by the early 1960s, as the FCC's own historians put it, the networks produced or bought the programme and sold time to the advertiser. That made ABC, CBS and NBC the sellers of a scarce, nationally simultaneous good, and the upfront the market where it cleared. Their leverage was structural: the FCC capped any owner at seven television stations (no more than five VHF) from 1954, so no network could own its way past the affiliate system, and prime time itself was a fixed number of minutes per night. In 1975 the three networks took $2.31 billion, 43.8% of all US television advertising and 8.3% of all US advertising. But television was never the biggest seller in the country in this era: newspapers took $8.23 billion in 1975, and their local retail plus classified base kept them the largest medium through 1978 and beyond. Newspaper ownership was consolidating - by 1975 some 176 groups owned 59% of roughly 1,800 dailies. The clearest casualties were the mass-circulation general magazines whose national reach television now undercut: the Saturday Evening Post ended weekly publication in February 1969, Look closed on 19 October 1971 after a $5 million revenue loss in 1970, and Life ended its weekly run in December 1972. Two intermediary layers stood between buyer and seller and took their cut: agencies at 15% of gross, and station representative firms at a negotiated 5-20% of what was left.

Graded C because the network share is a constructed ratio of two Coen subcategories; both inputs are read directly from the series. Interval covers the Television Factbook alternative TV total ($4,722M for 1975), which would raise the within-TV share but not the all-media share.

MEDIUM.summary: Television is the era's growth story and newspapers are its scale story. US television advertising went from $171 million in 1950 (3.0% of all spend) to $5,263 million in 1975 (18.9%), on the back of household penetration rising from 9.0% to 97.1%. Television passed radio and magazines in total spend in 1954 and passed national newspaper advertising the same year, but it never passed newspapers overall inside the era: newspapers took $8,234 million in 1975, 29.5% of all spend, and were still the largest medium in 1978 on S&P/McCann figures. The correct answer to 'when did television beat print' is therefore money-type specific: television won national money in 1954 and local money never, in this era. Even in national money the win was contested - direct mail, at $4,124 million in 1975, was the single largest national medium at era end, and television's national total exceeded direct mail only in 1968-1970 before the cigarette ban and the Prime Time Access Rule pushed it back. Radio survived by inverting itself: network radio collapsed from $196 million (1950) to $43 million (1960) while local spot radio grew sixfold, making radio a local retail medium. Classified grew from $377 million to $2,159 million and from 18% to 26% of newspaper revenue. Directory (Yellow Pages) advertising is the era's biggest data hole - Coen does not break it out until 1980 - but back-casting puts it near $1.5 billion in 1975, already larger than magazines' local business and roughly the size of radio.

SCALE.summary: US advertising spend rose from $5.70 billion in 1950 to $27.90 billion in 1975, a 4.9-fold nominal increase and a compound rate of about 6.6% a year. Measured against the economy the era peaks early and then declines: advertising was about 1.9% of GDP in 1950, about 2.2% around 1960, and 1.66% by 1975. That shape matters for the capture-versus-expansion argument, because television's entire rise happens while advertising is a shrinking share of national income - television took share from other media rather than enlarging the pot. The national/local balance shifted mildly towards local, from 57.2%/42.8% in 1950 to 54.5%/45.5% in 1975, as local retail and classified outgrew national brand budgets in the inflationary early 1970s. By money type the mix is remarkably stable: national brand 43.1% to 39.7%, local retail 36.2% to 37.8%, classified 6.6% to 7.7%, direct response 14.1% to 14.8%. No credible period source for world advertising expenditure could be found, so the global figure here is an explicit triangulation: roughly $54 billion in 1975, of which the United States was a little over half.

USPS Office of Inspector General, RARC-WP-16-006, 'Advertising Mail: Past and Present'

PRICING.summary: This is the era's mechanism change, and it happens in the middle of the era, not at its edges. Under sponsorship the advertiser bought a programme and the network sold time as a facilities charge; the price was negotiated per show and the advertiser carried the production risk. Pat Weaver's magazine concept at NBC (1949-56) broke that by selling participations inside network-owned shows such as Today and Tonight, and rising production costs made single sponsorship unaffordable for all but specials. The quiz-show scandals of 1958-59 finished the argument by making sponsor control of content a liability; by the early 1960s the networks produced or bought the programmes and sold the time. Once inventory was network-owned and fungible, three things followed. The unit shrank: the 60-second announcement became standard around 1960, advertisers piggybacked two 30s inside one minute through the 1960s, and the 30 became the standard purchase in the 1970-71 season. The clearing mechanism became annual: from 1962, when ABC concentrated its premieres in one September week to catch the car makers, the networks sold the coming season in a compressed spring window - the upfront. And the price became a rate per thousand rather than a fee per show: network prime-time cost per commercial minute went from about $30,000 in the early 1960s to $65,000 by 1970, quoted and negotiated against Nielsen households and, increasingly, Nielsen demographics. The intermediary stack was explicit and stable: media billed the agency gross, the agency kept 15% and could take a further 2% cash discount for prompt payment, and station representative firms took a negotiated 5-20% of what remained on national spot business. Classified and directory advertising ran on an entirely different pricing regime in the same years - self-serve, per agate line or per directory listing tier, annual contract, no agency and no commission.

claims.statement: The agency commission was 15% of gross media billings throughout the era: media billed the agency $2,500 gross, the agency paid $2,125 and billed the client $2,500.
claims.unit: percent of gross media billings

sources.name: Zeigler & Howard, 'Broadcast Advertising', 3rd ed. (1991)
Silk & Berndt, HBS Working Paper 11-039

claims.statement: On top of the 15%, agencies took a 2% cash discount on the net for paying media within about ten days - a second, smaller intermediary take that is usually omitted from take-rate comparisons.
claims.unit: percent cash discount on net media cost

sources.name: Zeigler & Howard, 'Broadcast Advertising', 3rd ed. (1991)

claims.statement: Station representative firms, which sold local stations' inventory to national advertisers, took a negotiated commission in a normal range of about 5-20%, calculated on the amount left after the agency's 15% had been deducted. The source publishes the range but no typical value, and notes that television averages ran below radio's.
claims.unit: percent commission to the station representative firm

sources.name: Zeigler & Howard, 'Broadcast Advertising: A Comprehensive Working Textbook', 3rd ed. (1991), via World Radio History

claims.method: Zeigler & Howard give the range 5-20% and the calculation base (net of the agency's 15%), but publish no central. Central 10 is the range midpoint and is a construction, not a source figure; because national spot television was the largest rep-sold category in this era and the source states TV averages ran below radio's, the television-weighted central probably sits below 10%.

claims.statement: Network prime-time advertising cost about $30,000 per commercial minute in the early 1960s and about $65,000 per commercial minute by 1970 - a 117% nominal increase across the decade.
claims.unit: USD per commercial minute of network prime time, 1970

sources.name: Zeigler & Howard, 'Broadcast Advertising', 3rd ed. (1991)

claims.statement: Derived network prime-time cost per thousand television households: roughly $3.30 per commercial minute in 1960 and roughly $5.90 in 1970 - the price of attention in the era's dominant national medium.
claims.unit: USD per thousand television households per commercial minute, 1970
claims.method: CPM = cost per commercial minute / (television households x average prime-time household rating / 1,000). 1970: $65,000 / (58.5m x 0.19 = 11.12m homes) = $5.85 per thousand. 1960: $30,000 / (45.75m x 0.20 = 9.15m homes) = $3.28 per thousand. Cost per minute from Zeigler & Howard; television households from Nielsen via TVB; the average prime-time household rating of 19-20 is an assumption, and the interval is generated by varying it from 15 to 25.

claims.statement: Published 30-second prices for the first Super Bowl (15 January 1967) run from $37,500 to $42,500. The two networks priced their simultaneous broadcasts differently: the documented per-minute rates were $85,000 on CBS and $75,000 on NBC, whose halves are $42,500 and $37,500. Secondary compilations also quote a flat $42,000 attributed to both networks. No single price applies to both broadcasts.
claims.unit: USD per 30-second spot

NBC, 'How Much a Super Bowl Ad Costs in 2023 Compared With History'

claims.method: Central 40,000 is the midpoint of the two networks' half-minute rates and is a construction, not a transacted price. Bounds are the two networks' own documented half-minute rates: NBC $75,000/2 = $37,500 and CBS $85,000/2 = $42,500. A less well attributed CBS figure of $45,500 circulates and is deliberately excluded for want of a traceable source.

claims.statement: The upfront mechanism the era created had become the dominant clearing method by the end of the 1970s: 75-80% of the network prime-time schedule for the 1979-80 season was sold in the upfront, at prices 15% or more above the previous season.
claims.unit: percent of network prime-time inventory sold in the upfront

sources.name: Congressional Research Service Report 80-130 E, 'Commercial Television Broadcasting'

claims.statement: The upfront market dates from 1962, when ABC concentrated all its premieres in one week after Labor Day to catch car makers launching new models and sold the season in advance; CBS and NBC followed, and by the mid-1960s premiere week and the spring selling window were fixed institutions.
claims.unit: year the network television upfront market formed

MEASUREMENT.summary: The spot market could not exist without a currency, and in this era the currency was Nielsen. Nielsen bought C. E. Hooper's national radio and television ratings business in March 1950 and thereafter faced no serious national competitor; Arbitron (American Research Bureau) competed locally. The technology was two-layered and the layering matters: a small meter panel - the Audimeter, about 1,100-1,200 households - measured whether a set was on and what it was tuned to, and separate diary panels supplied the age and sex breaks that turned households into demographics. The Nielsen Station Index brought diary measurement to local markets from 1954. In September 1973 the Storage Instantaneous Audimeter wired 1,200 homes to Nielsen's computer centre and cut national ratings turnaround from one or two weeks to about 36 hours, which is what made same-week repricing and make-goods practical. The known bias was structural: the counter was a commercial subscription business selling to both the sellers and the buyers of the thing it counted, and the sample was tiny relative to the dollars it priced. That produced the era's measurement crisis - Representative Oren Harris's House investigations subcommittee held public hearings on ratings methodology and accuracy from 5 March 1963 to 23 September 1964, and the industry pre-empted regulation by funding its own audit body, the Broadcast Rating Council, in 1964, with minimum standards effective 31 March 1964. That body, later the Media Rating Council, is the institutional answer to 'who audits the counter', and it set the American pattern of private, industry-funded verification that the digital platforms later inherit.

claims.statement: Nielsen acquired C. E. Hooper's national radio and television ratings business in March 1950, the transaction that gave one private firm the national broadcast audience currency for the whole era.
claims.unit: year Nielsen acquired Hooper's national ratings business

sources.name: EBSCO Research Starters, 'A. C. Nielsen Company: Pioneers in Marketing and Media Research'
NYU Libraries, radio ratings research guide (Crossley/CAB, Hooper, Nielsen succession)

claims.statement: The national metered panel behind every network television price in this era was about 1,200 households - roughly one metered home for every 54,000 US television homes in 1973.
claims.unit: metered households in the Nielsen national television panel

sources.name: Television Obscurities, 'Nielsen Black Weeks'
Museum of Broadcast Communications, 'Audimeter'
Television Bureau of Advertising, 'National Television Penetration Trends' (source: The Nielsen Company)

claims.statement: The Storage Instantaneous Audimeter, introduced in September 1973, cut national ratings turnaround to about 36 hours from the one to two weeks the previous system needed - the era's decisive measurement-speed change.
claims.unit: hours to produce national television ratings

sources.name: Television Obscurities, 'Nielsen Black Weeks'

claims.statement: The Harris hearings on broadcast ratings ran from 5 March 1963 to 23 September 1964 and produced the industry-funded Broadcast Rating Council in 1964. Its first minimum standards are reported to have taken effect on 31 March 1964 and the final committee report on 13 January 1966; both of those subsidiary dates rest on a single secondary source and are not corroborated by the MRC's own history.

claims.statement: One national household rating point was worth 685,000 television households in 1975, against 457,500 in 1960 - the unit in which network inventory was actually priced.
claims.unit: television households per national rating point

sources.name: Television Bureau of Advertising, 'National Television Penetration Trends' (source: The Nielsen Company)

TARGETING.summary: Targeting in this era is a story of two very different precisions running side by side. Broadcast targeting was coarse and got standardised rather than finer. Geography was fixed in 1966, when Nielsen defined Designated Market Areas and Arbitron defined Areas of Dominant Influence - about 220 markets, an average of a quarter of a million television households each - which turned national spot buying into a commodity that could be priced market by market. Demography arrived through Nielsen's diary panels: the buyable unit became an age and sex cell such as women 18-49 within a programme within a daypart, roughly a dozen standard cells. Multiplying the two gives an order of magnitude for how many distinct audiences an advertiser could actually purchase: a few thousand. The consequence was visible on screen. Once networks were priced on who was watching rather than how many, high-rating programmes with the wrong audience became worthless: CBS cancelled its rural comedies at the end of the 1970-71 season - the rural purge - even though several were still winning their time slots. Direct mail meanwhile already had the precision the rest of the market would spend fifty years chasing. The ZIP code, introduced on 1 July 1963, gave mailers a machine-readable geographic key, and rented and merged lists let a mailer address one household out of 70.5 million by name. Lester Wunderman named the practice 'direct marketing' in a 1967 speech and the Direct Mail Advertising Association renamed itself the Direct Mail/Marketing Association in 1973 - the measurable-response tradition acquiring an identity a decade before database marketing scaled it.

claims.statement: Arbitron created Areas of Dominant Influence in 1966, dividing the US into about 200 exclusive markets, and Nielsen's Designated Market Area system dates from the same mid-1960s period; roughly 200-210 markets standardised the geography in which spot television was bought and sold. The market count grew slowly, reaching 209 by the early 1990s.
claims.unit: designated market areas

sources.name: TV and Radio Schedules Wiki, 'Media market' (Arbitron ADIs first created 1966, dividing the US into 200 exclusive areas)
Precisely, 'Designated Market Areas (DMA) - Nielsen DMA maps' (current count only: 'over 200'; carries no creation date)

claims.statement: The average Designated Market Area contained about 279,000 television households in 1970 - the finest geographic unit a television advertiser could buy.
claims.unit: television households per average DMA
claims.method: 58,500,000 US television households in 1970 (Nielsen via TVB) divided by roughly 210 markets = 278,571. Interval varies the market count from 195 to 225, the documented range across the late 1960s and 1970s (Arbitron's ADI structure began at 200 in 1966 and reached 209 by the early 1990s).

sources.name: Television Bureau of Advertising, 'National Television Penetration Trends' (source: The Nielsen Company)
TV and Radio Schedules Wiki, 'Media market' (Arbitron ADIs first created 1966, dividing the US into 200 exclusive areas)

claims.statement: Broadcast targeting precision at the end of the era was of the order of 2,600 distinct purchasable audience segments - about 220 geographies crossed with about a dozen standard Nielsen age and sex cells.
claims.unit: distinct purchasable broadcast audience segments
claims.method: 220 DMAs x 12 standard demographic cells (children 2-11 and 6-11, teens 12-17, men and women 18-34, 18-49, 25-54, 55+, total adults) = 2,640. Interval varies the cell count from 8 to 20 and the market count from 190 to 225. This is an order-of-magnitude precision metric for cross-era comparison, not a figure reported by any period source.

sources.name: Precisely, 'Designated Market Areas (DMA) - Nielsen DMA maps'
Congressional Research Service Report 80-130 E (target-audience buying and cost per thousand)

events.title: Nielsen buys Hooper's national ratings business
events.desc: A. C. Nielsen acquires C. E. Hooper's national radio and television ratings service, ending the competitive ratings market that had characterised era 2 and installing a single private firm as the currency for every national broadcast price for the next twenty-five years.

events.title: Consent decree ends collective enforcement of the 15% commission
events.desc: Final judgment entered in United States v. American Association of Advertising Agencies et al. (complaint filed 12 May 1955, SDNY) against the AAAA and five publisher trade associations. It dismantled the 'recognition' system through which the trade bodies jointly enforced a fixed 15% commission and blocked rebating. The complaint covered only national print advertising, so direct mail and broadcast were untouched, and the 15% rate survived in practice for decades.

claim.statement: The advertising covered by the 1956 consent decree - national advertising in newspapers, magazines, business papers and farm publications, matching the six defendant associations - was 21% of total US advertising expenditure in 1956, which is why the decree changed the law without changing the price. Newspapers and magazines alone were only 15%.
claim.unit: percent of total US advertising expenditure covered by the consent decree

sources.name: Silk & Berndt, 'The Unbundling of Advertising Agency Services: An Economic Analysis', HBS Working Paper 11-039
U.S. Department of Justice, Antitrust Division: legacy antitrust judgment record, U.S. v. American Association of Advertising Agencies, Inc., et al.
Coen Structured Advertising Expenditure Dataset (CS Ad Dataset v1.14), workbook parsed independently by the verifier

events.title: Van Doren testifies; sponsor control of programming becomes untenable
events.desc: Charles Van Doren tells the House Subcommittee on Legislative Oversight he was 'involved, deeply involved, in a deception'. The quiz-show scandals - Dotto cancelled 15 August 1958, grand jury from late 1958, hearings from October 1959, the Communications Act amended 13 September 1960 to outlaw fixed contests - made advertiser control of content a legal and reputational liability. Combined with production costs the networks were better placed to absorb, it completed the handover of programming, and therefore of inventory, from advertisers to networks.

events.title: Interpublic incorporated: the first advertising holding company
events.desc: Marion Harper incorporates Interpublic as a holding company with McCann-Erickson as its largest subsidiary, explicitly modelled on General Motors' divisional structure. It solved the conflict-policy constraint that had capped agency size - one owner could now hold agencies serving competing clients - and set the template that Omnicom, WPP and Publicis follow after this era.

events.title: ABC concentrates premiere week and the upfront market forms
events.desc: ABC schedules all its new-season premieres in the week after Labor Day to align with car makers' model-year launches, and sells the season in advance. CBS and NBC follow. With inventory now network-owned and supply fixed by the length of prime time, a compressed spring selling window became the annual clearing event for national television - the upfront.

events.title: Harris ratings hearings produce the Broadcast Rating Council
events.desc: Representative Oren Harris's investigations subcommittee held public hearings on the methodology, accuracy and use of broadcast ratings from 5 March 1963 to 23 September 1964. Rather than regulate, the committee pushed the industry to fund its own auditor: the Broadcast Rating Council was founded in 1964, with minimum standards effective 31 March 1964, and the final committee report followed on 13 January 1966. It became the Media Rating Council and set the American pattern of private, industry-funded audience verification.

events.title: DMA and ADI standardise the spot-television map
events.desc: Nielsen defines Designated Market Areas and Arbitron defines Areas of Dominant Influence, roughly 220 markets ranked by television households. National spot advertising becomes a standardised, comparably priced commodity for the first time, and the geographic unit of American media buying is fixed for the next half-century.

events.title: Cigarette advertising banned from broadcast
events.desc: The Public Health Cigarette Smoking Act ban takes effect, removing from television and radio a category paying broadcasters roughly $225 million a year. Tobacco money moved to print, coupons and contests but total tobacco advertising fell. Television advertising declined in 1971 for the only time in the era, and the search for cheaper units accelerated the shift to the 30-second spot.

claim.statement: Cigarette advertising was about 4.6% of all US broadcast advertising expenditure in 1970 - roughly $225 million against $4,904 million of television plus radio spend - the largest single product category ever removed from a US medium by law.
claim.unit: percent of US broadcast advertising expenditure
claim.method: $225M of cigarette money to broadcasters (EBSCO) divided by Coen's 1970 television ($3,596M) plus radio ($1,308M) total of $4,904M = 4.59%. Lower bound uses the alternative $150M television-only figure that appears in some accounts. Upper bound covers the units mismatch: EBSCO's $225M is revenue TO broadcasters, net of the 15% agency commission, while the Coen denominator is gross advertiser expenditure; grossing up gives $264.7M and 5.40%. Cross-check: Nelson's five-media cigarette total for 1970 is $296.6M against $225M broadcast plus ~$50M print plus outdoor.

sources.name: EBSCO Research Starters, 'Cigarette Ads Are Banned from Broadcast Media'
Jon P. Nelson, 'Advertising Bans in the United States', EH.net Encyclopedia (Table 2: cigarette five-media advertising $296.6M in 1970)
Coen Structured Advertising Expenditure Dataset (CS Ad Dataset v1.14), workbook parsed independently by the verifier

events.title: Prime Time Access Rule takes effect; the 30 becomes the standard unit
events.desc: The FCC's Prime Time Access Rule, adopted in 1970, takes effect with the 1971-72 season and returns half an hour of weekday and Saturday prime time (7:30-8:00 p.m. Eastern) to affiliates, cutting the network prime block from four hours to three. Network supply shrank in the same year cigarette demand disappeared. The industry's answer, adopted across the 1970-71 season, was to sell the half-minute as the standard purchase rather than the minute - the unit that defines the era.

claim.statement: The Prime Time Access Rule, effective with the week of 13 September 1971, barred network affiliates in the top 50 markets from carrying more than three of the four prime-time hours (7-11 p.m. Eastern). On weekdays and Saturdays it returned 30 minutes a night (7:30-8:00 p.m. Eastern) to affiliates; under the original rule Sundays lost a full hour, in two blocks (7:00-7:30 and 10:30-11:00 p.m.). Though it bound only the top 50 markets, the networks complied nationwide.
claim.unit: minutes of prime time returned to affiliates per weekday night

sources.name: Congressional Research Service Report 80-130 E, 'Commercial Television Broadcasting'
Wikipedia, 'Prime Time Access Rule'

events.title: Storage Instantaneous Audimeter delivers overnight national ratings
events.desc: Nielsen wires 1,200 metered households directly to its computer centre, cutting national ratings turnaround from one or two weeks to about 36 hours and ending the periodic 'black weeks' when no national ratings existed. Faster counting made faster repricing possible: make-goods, scatter pricing and in-season audience guarantees all became administrable.

boundary_notes: HAND-OFF FROM ERA 2 (1949/1950, Coen CS Ad Dataset, $ millions): total US ad spend 5,210 (1949) and 5,700 (1950); newspapers 1,911/2,070; radio 571/605 (radio's all-time peak share is 11.0% in 1949, so radio is never the #1 US medium - era 2 should agree); television 58/171; direct mail 756/803; magazines 458/478. Television households were 9.0% of US households in 1950. Sponsorship was still the dominant network selling mode in 1950; Nielsen bought Hooper's national ratings business in March 1950, which is the measurement handover point between eras 2 and 3. HAND-OFF TO ERA 4 (1975/1976, same series): total 27,900 (1975) rising to 33,300 (1976); newspapers 8,234/9,618 and still the largest medium; television 5,263/6,721; direct mail 4,124/4,786; radio 1,980/2,330; magazines 1,465/1,789; business papers 919/1,035; billboards 335/383; Miscellaneous 5,506/6,552. National/local split 54.5%/45.5% in 1975. Newspaper classified 2,159 in 1975 (HSUS De523-526). Advertising was 1.66% of GDP in 1975. Era 4 should start from these, and should note three things this era hands it unfinished: (1) Yellow Pages is not separately reported in the Coen series until 1980, when it appears at 2,900 - era 3's 1975 estimate of roughly 1,500 is a documented back-cast, not a series value, and era 4 owns the first sourced directory number; (2) the 15% commission is alive and dominant at the era boundary (71% of large national advertisers still on commission in 1982), so era 4 must not date its death to the 1970s - the a la carte and media-buying-service pressure that begins in the early 1970s is a precursor, not the break; (3) the upfront mechanism era 3 created was clearing 75-80% of network prime-time inventory by the 1979-80 season, at prices 15%+ above the prior season. Media shares at the boundary, on S&P Industry Surveys figures drawn from McCann-Erickson data: newspapers 30.1% (1972) falling to 29.0% (1978); television 17.6% (1972) rising to 20.2% (1978); national advertising 55% of the market in 1978. Two era-4 items that belong to era 4 and not here: the 1987 People Meter, and PRIZM, whose launch date sources place variously at 1974 and 1978 - era 4 should resolve that conflict rather than inherit it. Cross-era measurement chain: audited circulation (ABC, 1914, era 1) to Crossley/Hooper (era 2) to Nielsen plus the Broadcast Rating Council (era 3) to the People Meter (era 4). Cross-era money-type note: the four-way split used here (national brand / local retail / classified / direct response) is constructed to partition the Coen total exactly, using Coen's national and local totals, Coen's direct mail line and the HSUS classified line; sibling eras should use the same construction so the money-type ribbon is continuous.
